cves.d: A flaw was found in the GNU Binutils BFD library, a widely used component for handling binary files such as object files and executables. The issue occurs when processing specially crafted XCOFF object files, where a relocation type value is not properly validated before being used. This can cause the program to read memory outside of intended bounds. As a result, affected tools may crash or expose unintended memory contents, leading to denial-of-service or limited information disclosure risks.

PHP has various global state that temporarily points into request memory. In some scenarios, global state may not be correctly reset, or may be repopulated after being reset. The global state may then refer to request memory even after it has been freed. Subsequent requests may read or branch on this stale state before it is fully initialized. Multiple strategies can trigger this condition and produce remote code execution (RCE).

PHP uses longjmp() for out-of-memory (OOM) errors to exit the current context and abort handling of the request. Some contexts may not properly account for this scenario and leave request memory in an uninitialized state before performing an allocation. The subsequent request cleanup procedure may read or branch on this memory. Multiple OOM strategies can consistently trigger this condition and lead to remote code execution (RCE).

The rsyslog's`imuxsock` special parser can end up writing into the received message raw buffer when trying to replace the message timestamp with the system's timestamp. A local attacker with the ability to write to the `imuxsock` socket can leverage that by crafting a malformed PRI value with a short timestamp to lead the rsyslog to perform the out-of-bounds write.

A flaw was found in dbus. A local attacker can exploit this vulnerability by connecting to an affected service, requesting a response, and stopping socket reads while keeping the connection open. Because the socket transport handles broken pipe write errors as retryable, the application enters a continuous retry loop. This can lead to excessive CPU consumption, resulting in a denial of service (DoS) for the target process.

A flaw was found in dbus when configured with the nonce-tcp transport. An unauthenticated attacker able to connect to an exposed listener can cause a Denial of Service (DoS) by opening a connection and withholding the expected authentication token. Because the server processes this verification without enforcing a timeout, the stalled connection blocks the accept process and prevents legitimate clients from establishing new connections.

A flaw was found in D-Bus. In configurations where the daemon falls back to using the Unix select() mechanism for event monitoring, it does not verify whether file descriptor numbers exceed allocated limits. A local attacker can exploit this flaw by opening a large number of concurrent connections to trigger an out-of-bounds write on the stack. This can cause the daemon to crash, resulting in a Denial of Service (DoS).

A flaw was found in SSSD's PAM responder. A local attacker can send an authentication request without first negotiating the client protocol version. The responder dereferences a NULL protocol-version pointer and crashes, disrupting SSSD-backed authentication. Repeated crafted requests can sustain the denial of service.

A flaw was found in SSSD's PAM responder on builds with the JSON PAM extension enabled. A local attacker can submit a crafted authentication request containing a non-string OAuth2 code value. Missing JSON type validation leads to a NULL pointer dereference, terminating the PAM responder and disrupting SSSD-backed authentication.

A flaw was found in SSSD's conversion of X.509 certificate RSA public keys to SSH keys. Missing size checks before copying RSA components into fixed-size stack buffers can cause a stack buffer overflow. An attacker able to supply a certificate with oversized RSA components that passes the configured certificate checks can cause denial of service and corrupt SSH responder memory.

A flaw was found in cpio. A local user can cause a Denial of Service (DoS) by triggering a stack-based buffer overflow when creating archives in tar or ustar formats. When archiving files owned by users or groups with names exceeding 32 characters, cpio copies these names into fixed-size memory without verifying their length. This unbounded copy corrupts stack memory and causes the application to crash.

A flaw was found in QEMU's NBD block driver. A malicious NBD server can send an incomplete structured read reply marked as done, causing QEMU to return uninitialized host heap memory to the guest VM, resulting in host memory disclosure.

A flaw was found in OpenSCAP. This vulnerability allows for information disclosure when performing offline scans of untrusted filesystem images, such as container images or virtual machine (VM) disks. Because the scanner does not properly restrict symbolic link (symlink) resolution to the target image's root directory, an attacker can supply a crafted image containing links pointing to files on the host system. When the scan runs, typically with elevated privileges, OpenSCAP follows these links to read sensitive host files and expose their contents in the scan report or manipulate compliance results.

A flaw was found in libstdc++. When a byte-by-byte write operation fails during file stream processing, the library may still append data into the internal memory buffer. An attacker capable of inducing repeated write failures in an affected service can trigger a buffer overflow, potentially resulting in a Denial of Service (DoS) or memory corruption.

A flaw was found in GStreamer's gst-plugins-bad MPEG Program Stream demuxer and resindvd DVD-playback plugin. The PES header parsers do not adequately check remaining data before reading timestamps and optional header fields. Opening a specially crafted MPEG Program Stream file can cause an out-of-bounds read and potentially crash the application, resulting in a denial of service.

A flaw was found in the GStreamer gst-plugins-bad MXF plugin. Insufficient bounds checks when parsing crafted VANC data can cause an out-of-bounds read in the demuxer, while an incorrect buffer size calculation when muxing multiple ancillary packets can cause an out-of-bounds write. Processing affected content may crash the application, resulting in a denial of service.

A flaw was found in cockpit-storaged. A Tang keyserver address read from a clevis token in a LUKS header is concatenated into curl's argument vector without a "--" separator. An address beginning with "-" is parsed by curl as an option instead of a hostname, allowing an attacker who can attach a crafted LUKS/clevis block device (for example, a local unprivileged user with an active console or desktop login session) to have an administratively-privileged Cockpit user unknowingly trigger curl option injection when editing the device's Tang keyserver settings. This can lead to arbitrary file read or write as the Cockpit session user.

A flaw was found in QEMU's NBD server. A remote attacker can crash qemu-nbd, qemu-storage-daemon, or qemu-system by sending NBD_OPT_SET_META_CONTEXT or NBD_OPT_LIST_META_CONTEXT with a declared option length exceeding the actual payload, triggering an assertion failure and denial of service.

cves.d: A flaw was found in GStreamer's gst-plugins-good MOV/MP4 demuxer. When processing an uncompressed video track, qtdemux fails to validate the declared row alignment and chroma geometry before using them to build a video buffer layout. A crafted file can cause an out-of-bounds heap read while the sample is copied, potentially crashing the application and causing denial of service.

A flaw was found in the SRT and WebVTT subtitle parser in GStreamer's gst-plugins-base. While sanitizing inline subtitle markup, the parser repeatedly searches the remaining text with unanchored regular expressions. A crafted subtitle cue with a long line of unmatched markup-like text can force quadratic CPU use and make a GStreamer-based application unresponsive.

A flaw was found in QEMU's NBD server. A remote attacker can crash a multi-export NBD server process by exploiting stale metadata export state during an extended BLOCK_STATUS request, resulting in an assertion failure and denial of service.

A flaw was found in the default seccomp profile used by Podman via containers-common. Deny rules for AF_VSOCK and NETLINK_AUDIT compared socket arguments with unmasked 64-bit equality. Because the kernel truncates those int arguments to 32 bits, setting upper bits can bypass the deny rules.

A flaw was found in GStreamer's gst-plugins-bad package. When processing a specially crafted H.264 video file containing malformed MVC or SVC extension slice NAL units, a 1-byte heap out-of-bounds read can occur during parsing. This happens when the parser attempts to check slice boundary information without first verifying that the NAL unit contains enough data beyond the extension header. An attacker could exploit this by tricking a user into opening a malicious H.264 video file, potentially causing the application to crash or leak a single byte of heap memory.

A flaw was found in the GStreamer gst-plugins-bad package. When processing a malformed H.266/VVC video stream with a crafted aspect ratio indicator value, the H.266 parser performs an out-of-bounds read of up to 8 bytes from adjacent memory. This flaw allows an attacker to craft a malicious H.266 video file or stream that, when processed by a GStreamer-based application, could leak limited memory contents through video metadata, potentially exposing sensitive information from the application's address space.

A heap-based buffer overflow was found in dnsmasq. When DNSSEC validation and
query logging are both enabled, logging of DS or DNSKEY replies containing
unsupported algorithm or digest types can cause dnsmasq to write past the end
of an internal logging buffer. A remote attacker able to supply such a DNS
response may crash the dnsmasq process, resulting in denial of service.

A flaw was found in sssd. When authenticating with a YubiKey, the SSSD PAM responder can crash due to a use-after-free vulnerability, where a memory pointer is incorrectly handled. A local attacker could exploit this flaw by manipulating smartcard or YubiKey contents, leading to a denial of service that disrupts authentication. This vulnerability also presents a potential for privilege escalation, although it is difficult to exploit.

The fix for CVE-2026-2443 was regressed by a subsequent rework commit that replaced specific overflow checks with a general signed comparison. When a client sends a Range request with a suffix length exceeding the content size, the resulting negative start value is not properly clamped, leading to malformed HTTP 206 responses and log flooding.

A heap out-of-bounds read flaw was found in libsoup. When parsing multipart HTTP messages, an integer type mismatch between the caller and soup_headers_parse() can cause the length parameter to be incorrectly truncated, leading to a heap buffer over-read. A remote attacker could use this flaw to crash an application using libsoup or potentially disclose heap memory contents.

The fix for CVE-2026-0716 (commit 6ff7ef0, libsoup 3.6.6) placed the integer overflow guard inside the if (masked) block, leaving unmasked server-to-client frames unprotected. A malicious WebSocket server can send a crafted unmasked frame with a payload length near UINT64_MAX to trigger an OOB read in a libsoup-based client when max_incoming_payload_size is set to 0.

A heap buffer overflow issue exists in the rms_mqtt daemon on Teltonika Networks devices. An authenticated attacker with access to the affected service could trigger a heap-based buffer overflow, resulting in a denial of service. This issue affects RUT: from 7.0 through 7.18.0; RUTX: from 7.0 through 7.18.0; RUTM: from 7.0 through 7.18.0; RUTC: from 7.0 through 7.18.0; ATRM: from 7.16.1 through 7.18.0; TRB: from 7.0 through 7.18.0; OTD: from 7.11.1 through 7.18.0; TAP: from 7.4.3 through 7.18.0; DAP: from 7.12 through 7.18.0; SWM: from 1.6.3 through 1.7.1; TSW: from 1.1 through 1.7.1.

Issue summary: A QUIC peer that sends many small out-of-order STREAM fragments
while withholding the first byte of the stream may cause OpenSSL to buffer
a large number of reassembly nodes occupying much larger memory than
the actual data sent.

Impact summary: A remote peer can pin large amounts of memory on a server that
accepts incoming QUIC streams, potentially exhausting memory and causing
Denial of Service.

CWE: CWE-770: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling

Description: QUIC receive flow control limits the highest byte offset a peer
may reach on a stream. It does not limit how many out-of-order fragments the
receiver buffers. OpenSSL allocates a reassembly node for each non-adjacent
STREAM fragment and never caps the count. A peer that opens a stream and sends
many one-byte fragments at increasing offsets, while withholding the first
byte, makes the receiver retain one node per fragment without delivering any
data.

Only applications that accept incoming streams are exposed. With the default
policy, which rejects peer-initiated streams, the stream is torn down before
state accumulates. Because the read side never advances past the missing
prefix, the flow control window never slides and the nodes stay pinned for the
life of the connection.

The per-stream window bounds the highest offset, so the memory one stream can
pin is finite, but it can reach tens of megabytes and, across many streams and
connections, drive memory pressure and Denial of Service. The severity is
limited because the exhaustion is bounded by flow control and requires a
non-default configuration.

FIPS impact: no
The affected code is outside the FIPS module boundary.

Issue summary: Verifying a maliciously crafted CMS or PKCS#7 SignedData
message with CRL checking enabled may consume excessive CPU time, growing with
the square of the message size.

Impact summary: An attacker who can submit a CMS or PKCS#7 SignedData message
to an application that verifies it with CRL checking enabled can occupy a CPU
core for seconds to minutes, causing Denial of Service. Applications that
leave CRL checking disabled are not affected.

CWE: CWE-407: Inefficient Algorithmic Complexity

Description: With CRL checking enabled, OpenSSL compares each CRL distribution
point of a certificate against the issuing distribution point of every
candidate CRL. For a nameRelativeToCRLIssuer distribution point, the full name
is the CRL issuer name with the relative name appended. Since the change that
deferred this computation, crl_crldp_check() rebuilds that full name for each
candidate CRL and frees it again.

CMS_verify() and PKCS7_verify() take both the distribution points and the
candidate CRLs from the message, and this scoring runs before any signature is
checked. An application is exposed only if it sets X509_V_FLAG_CRL_CHECK on
the store and does not pass CMS_NOCRL or PKCS7_NOCRL; CRL checking is off by
default. In TLS the CRLs come from the local store, so a peer controls only
the distribution point count.

The cost grows with the product of the distribution point count, the CRL count
and the issuer name length, all chosen by the message author; a few hundred
kilobytes can occupy a CPU core for tens of seconds. Verification still fails
as it should, with no crash, no incorrect result and no memory growth.
Requiring CRL checking is what limits the severity.

FIPS impact: no
The affected code is outside the FIPS module boundary.

Issue summary: The QUIC stack queues a RETIRE_CONNECTION_ID frame also for
retransmitted NEW_CONNECTION_ID frames. This allows a remote malicious
QUIC stack to queue an unlimited number of RETIRE_CONNECTION_ID frames.

Impact summary: A malicious remote QUIC peer can trigger an out-of-memory
condition causing a Denial of Service.

CWE: CWE-770: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling

Description: The earlier fix for CVE-2026-84784 was not complete. It
failed to ignore retransmissions of the NEW_CONNECTION_ID frame. The QUIC
implementation created and inserted a RETIRE_CONNECTION_ID frame for every
retransmitted NEW_CONNECTION_ID frame it received and there was no limit
on how many RETIRE_CONNECTION_ID frames were queued.

This issue allows a malicious remote QUIC stack to trigger an unbounded
allocation of memory and eventually an out-of-memory (OOM) condition.

FIPS impact: no
The FIPS module is not affected as the QUIC implementation is outside the
OpenSSL FIPS module boundary.

Issue summary: A DANE-enabled TLS client may crash by dereferencing a NULL
pointer when processing an unusual combination of certificate and TLSA
records.

Impact summary: The impact is limited to a client crash (potential Denial
of Service).

CWE: CWE-476: NULL Pointer Dereference

Description: A DANE-enabled TLS client that supports TLSA records with at
least one of the PKIX-TA(0) or PKIX-EE(1) usages alongside the DANE-TA(2)
usage may crash by dereferencing a NULL pointer if the server claims a trusted
CA's certificate to be its end-entity certificate and has an unusual mix of
associated TLSA records.

DANE SMTP clients should not be affected since only the
DANE-TA(2) and DANE-EE(3) TLSA record usages are specified applicable
in SMTP.  For example, the Postfix MTA is not affected, while the Exim
MTA does not at present use OpenSSL's DANE implementation.

Use of DANE in validation of RFC7250 raw public keys (RPKs) is also
unaffected, as these only use DANE-EE(3) TLSA records.

Only applications that support combining the DANE PKI with a traditional PKI
are potentially affected.  A DANE-enabled browser or similar, that uses
OpenSSL's DANE API could be affected.

FIPS impact: no
The DANE API is outside the FIPS module boundary.

Multiple out-of-bounds read vulnerabilities were found in GStreamer's pcapparse element. Malformed PCAP records can trigger reads beyond buffer boundaries during IPv4/TCP header parsing. This element is primarily used in debugging pipelines, limiting real-world exposure. A local attacker could trick a user into processing a specially crafted PCAP file, potentially leading to a crash or information disclosure.

A denial of service vulnerability was found in GStreamer's AV1 codec parser in gst-plugins-bad. The gst_av1_parser_parse_tile_list_obu() function passes a byte count to a bit-reader API that expects a bit count, causing parser desynchronization. A remote attacker could trick a user into opening a specially crafted AV1 media file, triggering an assertion abort and causing the application to crash.

A Denial of Service (DoS) vulnerability exists in the ARQ SPARQL Query Optimiser in Apache Jena ARQ prior to version 6.3.0 that allows a SPARQL query to use that cause excessive memory usage.
Users are recommended to upgrade to version 6.3.0, which fixes this issue.






Users who are unable to upgrade immediately, especially those who operate a public facing SPARQL service/application backed by Apache Jena are recommended to configure the ARQ symbol arq:optPathFlatten=false in their SPARQL execution context which disables the problematic optimisation.

Missing Authorization vulnerability in the public project REST API of Apache Texera (incubating).



The public project API did not check that a project had been made public before granting the caller read access to it. Any authenticated user with an approved account (the REGULAR or ADMIN role; new accounts need administrator approval by default) could give themselves lasting read access to other users' private projects and to the private workflows in them, including their version and execution history. Only deployments in which users have created projects are affected; the project feature is hidden in the web UI by default.



This issue affects Apache Texera: from 1.1.0-incubating before 1.3.0-incubating.



Users are recommended to upgrade to version 1.3.0-incubating, which fixes the issue by removing the deprecated project feature and its data.



If you cannot upgrade immediately, configure the reverse proxy in front of Texera to reject every request whose path starts with /api/project, /api/public/project or /api/access/project, and every request whose path contains ';', which the Texera server ignores when routing. Respond with 403 or 404, not 401: from 1.2.0-incubating the web UI treats a 401 as an expired session, and the workflow pages request the project list when they load. Unless an administrator has enabled the project feature, this does not affect other functionality; those project-list requests are simply rejected. Make sure the Texera server is reachable only through that proxy.



Blocking and upgrading do not undo access obtained earlier. Before upgrading, review the project_user_access table, which remains empty unless someone has used the feature: treat any READ grant on a project that is not listed in public_project, and that the project's owner did not give, as suspect. The upgrade deletes this table. Removing a grant does not remove copies the user may already have made of the workflows.

Missing Authorization vulnerability in the project REST API of Apache Texera (incubating).



The project API did not check that the caller owns, or has been granted access to, the project being accessed. Any authenticated user with an approved account (the REGULAR or ADMIN role; new accounts need administrator approval by default) could view, modify or delete other users' projects, change which workflows those projects contain, and see the e-mail addresses of a project's owner and collaborators. The project feature is hidden in the web UI by default, but the API was reachable regardless of that setting.



This issue affects Apache Texera: from 1.1.0-incubating before 1.3.0-incubating.



Users are recommended to upgrade to version 1.3.0-incubating, which fixes the issue by removing the deprecated project feature and its data.



If you cannot upgrade immediately, configure the reverse proxy in front of Texera to reject every request whose path starts with /api/project, /api/public/project or /api/access/project, and every request whose path contains ';', which the Texera server ignores when routing. Respond with 403 or 404, not 401: from 1.2.0-incubating the web UI treats a 401 as an expired session, and the workflow pages request the project list when they load. Unless an administrator has enabled the project feature, this does not affect other functionality; those project-list requests are simply rejected. Make sure the Texera server is reachable only through that proxy.



Blocking and upgrading do not undo access obtained earlier. Before upgrading, review the project, project_user_access and workflow_of_project tables, which remain empty unless someone has used the feature, and remove rows you do not expect; the upgrade deletes these tables. Do not copy project grants into workflow_user_access without checking each one.

Missing Authorization vulnerability in the computing unit workflow websocket of Apache Texera (incubating) allows an authenticated user to view workflow results, control workflow executions, and run code in a computing unit they have not been granted. In local JVM and single-node Docker Compose deployments this is possible directly; in Kubernetes deployments it is possible from code running inside another computing unit in the cluster.



This issue affects Apache Texera : from 1.1.0 through 1.2.0.



Users are recommended to upgrade to version 1.3.0, which fixes the issue. Local JVM and Docker Compose deployments do not provide the full security model and should only be used by trusted users.

An API which can allow a user to delete any workflow execution results is missing authentication. This means that any workflow result could be deleted by someone able to reach the Texera instance.



This issue affects Apache Texera: from 1.1.0-incubating before 1.3.0-incubating.



Users are recommended to upgrade to version 1.3.0-incubating, which fixes the issue.

Description

When StormCrawler fetches a host's `/robots.txt` and receives a redirect, `HttpRobotRulesParser`
resolves the `Location` header and re-fetches the target for up to five hops. The loop checks neither
the scheme, the host nor the port of the resolved target, and it is not governed by
`http.allow.redirects`, which only affects the page fetch. A crawled site can therefore point the
robots.txt fetch at any address reachable from the fetcher worker, including loopback interfaces,
private ranges and cloud metadata endpoints. Every crawled URL triggers a robots.txt fetch on a cache
miss, so no unusual configuration is required to reach the loop.

The fetched body is only parsed as robots rules and is not returned to the caller, so the read itself
is blind. The more direct impact is on credentials: the okhttp protocol applies its configured request
headers, including the `Authorization` header built from `http.basicauth.user` and
`http.basicauth.password` and anything in `http.custom.headers`, to every request it makes. Because
StormCrawler follows the redirect itself and issues a new request, okhttp's own removal of the
`Authorization` header across a host change does not apply, and the operator's crawl credentials are
delivered to the host the redirect names.

The connection-time IP filter, `http.filter.ipaddress.include` and `http.filter.ipaddress.exclude`, is
installed as an okhttp network interceptor on the same client and does apply to these hops when it is
configured. It ships with no rules, which is why the path is reachable in a default configuration. URL
filtering never applies, because the robots.txt fetch does not pass through the outlink filter chain.

Mitigation

Upgrade to 4.0.0, where a robots.txt redirect is followed only when the target uses http or https and
shares scheme, host and port with the URL it was reached from. Deployments that legitimately serve
robots.txt through a cross-host redirect can restore the previous behaviour with
`http.robots.redirect.crosshost.allow`.

Users who cannot upgrade immediately should set `http.filter.ipaddress.exclude` to cover loopback,
private, link-local and CGNAT ranges, which is enforced after DNS resolution and therefore also on
redirect hops. Operators who configure `http.basicauth.*` or `http.custom.headers` for a crawl should
assume those credentials may have been sent to third-party hosts and rotate them, and should scope
credentials by running a separate topology per origin.

Credit

Independently reported to the Apache StormCrawler PMC by n0mi1k, with a proof of concept.

Also found by the ASF -- using Claude agents to study the security of open-source projects, validated
and reported by Apache StormCrawler.

Description

The SQL status backend serialises per-URL metadata into a single column by concatenating a tabulation,
the key, an equals sign and the value, with no escaping. On read-back the string is split on the same
two characters, so the round trip is not injective: a value that contains a tabulation returns as one
or more additional keys that were never written.

Values on that path are supplied by crawled servers. `FetcherBolt` records the raw `Location` header of
a redirect as `_redirTo`, and `_redirTo` is part of the default `metadata.persist` set, so a redirect
whose `Location` contains a tabulation followed by `key=value` pairs introduces those keys into the
crawler's own control metadata on the next scheduling cycle. Several control keys are read without a
prefix, so the injected keys are live: `http.proxy.host`, `http.proxy.port`, `http.proxy.user` and
`http.proxy.pass` among them, as well as scheduling and request-shaping keys such as `depth`,
`max.depth`, `crawl.delay`, `http.content.limit` and `isSitemap`.

Where a proxy manager is configured, the consequence is not limited to corrupted scheduling data.
`SingleProxyManager.getProxy(Metadata)` consults the per-URL metadata first and returns what it finds,
so an injected proxy host and port take precedence over the operator's configured proxy and subsequent
fetches, together with any configured `Authorization` header, are routed through a host the crawled
content chose. A related defect in `AbstractStatusUpdaterBolt` compounds this: an injected
`status.store.as.is.with.nextfetchdate` that is not a valid instant escapes the enclosing try/catch and
stops the bolt, and because the stored row is replayed the failure repeats.

Deployments using the OpenSearch or Solr status backends are unaffected, because those serialise
metadata structurally.

Mitigation

Upgrade to 4.0.0, where the metadata column is written in an escaped form behind a format marker, rows
written by earlier versions are still decoded unchanged, and the stored next-fetch-date is parsed
defensively.

The fix does not repair rows written before the upgrade. Operators using the SQL status backend should
inspect the metadata column of an existing status table for tabulation characters and remove the
affected rows, and should assume any proxy credentials configured for the crawl may have been exercised
through an attacker-chosen proxy and rotate them. Users who cannot upgrade immediately can remove
`_redirTo` from `metadata.persist` to close the demonstrated path, though other crawled values reaching
persisted metadata remain.

Credit

Independently reported to the Apache StormCrawler PMC by n0mi1k, with a proof of concept.

Also found by the ASF -- using Claude agents to study the security of open-source projects, validated
and reported by Apache StormCrawler.

Description

`CookieConverter.getCookies` decides which stored cookies to attach to an outbound request. The
applicability check is nested inside a test for the presence of a `Domain` attribute, so a cookie
without one, which is the ordinary form of a session cookie, skips scoping entirely and is returned for
whatever target URL was passed. RFC 6265 requires the opposite: a cookie with no `Domain` attribute is
host-only and belongs to the host that set it.

Two further defects sit in the same method. The domain comparison has no notion of a registrable
domain, so a `Domain` value of `com` matches every host under it, and the comparison returns true when
it throws, so a failure to evaluate the check admits the cookie. Neither the converter nor
`MetadataTransfer`, which carries the stored cookie to outlinks, ever considers the host that issued
it.

Cookie handling is opt-in: it requires `http.use.cookies` to be set to true, which is not the default,
and the cookie key to be listed in `metadata.transfer`. The documented recipe does not work as written,
because the `metadata.transfer` example in the internals documentation names `set-cookie` while the key
present in metadata is `protocol.set-cookie` and the transfer matches key names exactly. Deployments
affected are therefore those where an operator determined the correct key, enabled cookie handling and
crawls an authenticated site whose pages link or redirect to other hosts. In that case the session
cookie of the authenticated origin is sent to those hosts.

Mitigation

Upgrade to 4.0.0, where a cookie without a `Domain` attribute is sent only to the host that set it, a
single-label domain is rejected and the domain check fails closed. Because the protocol does not yet
record the host that issued a cookie, cookies without a `Domain` attribute are not sent at all until
that host is recorded; operators relying on cookie transfer will notice this. The documentation error
is corrected in the same release.

Users who cannot upgrade immediately should confine an authenticated crawl to a topology whose URL
filters keep it on the origin that issued the credentials, and should not rely on cookie scoping as a
boundary. Rotating session credentials used for such crawls is advisable.

Credit

Independently reported to the Apache StormCrawler PMC by n0mi1k, with a proof of concept.

Also found by the ASF -- using Claude agents to study the security of open-source projects, validated
and reported by Apache StormCrawler.

Description

`HostURLFilter.configure` reads the `ignoreOutsideDomain` parameter but tests the node belonging to
`ignoreOutsideHost` when deciding whether the domain mode was configured. A filter configuration that
names only `ignoreOutsideDomain`, which the class documentation presents as an independent mode, is
therefore discarded: the flag is forced to false, `filter` short-circuits on its guard and every URL is
returned unchanged. The filter enforces nothing while appearing to be configured, and the failure is
silent. The mirror-image configuration, naming only `ignoreOutsideHost`, fails with a
`NullPointerException` while the topology is starting.

The effect is the loss of a scope control the operator configured, so a crawled page's outlinks are
followed to hosts the operator intended to exclude. Impact beyond crawl scope depends on what the
crawler then fetches and is not claimed here. Projects generated from the StormCrawler Maven archetypes
are not affected, because all three shipped filter configurations set both parameters.

Mitigation

Upgrade to 4.0.0, where each parameter is tested independently. Operators whose configuration sets only
`ignoreOutsideDomain` will find the crawl restricted to the source domain, as configured, which may
reduce the number of outlinks accepted.

Users who cannot upgrade immediately should set both `ignoreOutsideHost` and `ignoreOutsideDomain`
explicitly in the `HostURLFilter` configuration, which produces the intended behaviour on affected
versions.

Independently reported to the Apache StormCrawler PMC by n0mi1k, with a proof of concept.

Also found by the ASF -- using Claude agents to study the security of open-source projects, validated
and reported by Apache StormCrawler.

A flaw was found in Undertow, an HTTP server, within its HTTP response header writing path. The `writeString()` method performs a silent narrowing cast from 16-bit Unicode characters to 8-bit bytes when writing HTTP response header values. A remote attacker can exploit this by supplying specific Unicode characters in user-controlled input that an application places into response headers. This can lead to the truncation of these characters into ASCII control characters or special symbols, potentially resulting in limited integrity impact or information disclosure if the application does not properly sanitize user input.

cves.d:
The 'podman quadlet install --replace' command opens the existing destination file with O_CREATE|O_WRONLY but omits O_TRUNC. When the initial reflink copy attempt fails (common on non-reflink-capable filesystems including many RHEL default XFS configurations), the fallback in ReflinkOrCopy uses io.Copy which performs a non-truncating write. If the original Quadlet is larger than the new Quadlet, the file is not truncated and content from the original is preserved. The command completes with no warning.

There is no risk of information leakage as the user already had access to the Quadlet in order to replace it, and in most cases, this would only lead to invalid Quadlet files. However, security-related options from the end of the old Quadlet could be included in the new Quadlet, and if the truncation resulted in a valid Quadlet file, this could result in undesirable behavior. For example, running podman quadlet install --replace to remove a single line from the end of a Quadlet - including security-sensitive content, like AddCapability - will fail, and the option will continue to be used. Further, with Volume Quadlets, this can include additional mounts which can cause content to be unintentionally exposed into containers. If, later, the image is updated then compromised content might be leaked to an attacker.

The vulnerable code paths are in pkg/domain/infra/abi/quadlet.go (lines 338-360, O_CREATE|O_WRONLY without O_TRUNC) and vendor/go.podman.io/storage/pkg/fileutils/reflink_linux.go (lines 12-19, non-truncating io.Copy fallback).

A flaw was found in libdm. A local attacker could craft a malicious Logical Volume Manager (LVM) metadata configuration with deeply nested structures. This could lead to uncontrolled recursion in the libdm configuration file parser, exhausting the stack and causing any LVM command reading the metadata to crash. This vulnerability results in a Denial of Service (DoS) for affected systems.

Multiple Use-After-Free vulnerabilities were found in the add_archive_element function in ld/ldmain.c of the GNU linker (ld), a component of binutils. The root cause is that plugin_maybe_claim() in ld/plugin.c frees the original BFD object via bfd_close/_bfd_delete_bfd when entry->the_bfd->my_archive == NULL, but the caller retains both the original abfd parameter and a shallow copy (orig_input.the_bfd) as dangling pointers. These dangling pointers are subsequently dereferenced at three distinct locations in add_archive_element:

1. Line ~1442: accessing abfd->my_archive via bfd_usrdata(abfd->my_archive)
2. Line ~1493: multiple accesses to abfd and abfd->my_archive in a conditional check and bfd_get_filename call
3. Line ~1525: dereferencing the shallow copy orig_input.the_bfd->my_archive in trace/verbose logging

The vulnerability is triggered when LTO plugins are active (link_info.lto_plugin_active is true) and the input object has abfd->my_archive == NULL, which is a valid state for standalone object files. Red Hat builds binutils with --enable-plugins and --enable-lto, confirming the vulnerable code path is compiled in and reachable.

An attacker who can supply a crafted object or archive file to a build process using LTO-enabled linking could exploit this flaw to cause a denial of service (linker crash via segmentation fault). Arbitrary code execution is theoretically possible through heap manipulation but is substantially mitigated by hardening measures including stack protector, FORTIFY_SOURCE, ASLR, and PIE.

The attack surface is limited to build-time environments — the linker is a development tool not exposed in production runtime. The most realistic exploitation scenario is a supply chain attack introducing a crafted object file as a build dependency in CI/CD pipelines or development environments.

A flaw was found in 389 Directory Server. The CleanAllRUV and Abort CleanAllRUV replication-maintenance extended operations perform no authorization check, allowing an unauthenticated remote attacker to invoke them when nsslapd-allow-anonymous-access is enabled (the default), or any authenticated low-privilege user to invoke them otherwise. This allows removal of a replica ID from replication metadata, purging of changelog records, and interruption of administrator-initiated cleanup, which can leave replication inconsistent or unavailable.

A flaw was found in insights-core where the password redaction layer fails to recognize credentials not keyed under the literal string 'password'. This allows SSSD LDAP bind passwords (ldap_default_authtok) and Pacemaker fence device credentials to be included in cleartext in archives uploaded to console.redhat.com.

cves.d: A TOCTOU (Time-of-Check-Time-of-Use) race condition vulnerability was found in the fixfiles script in policycoreutils. When running fixfiles relabel or fixfiles restore, the script used find and chcon commands to locate and relabel unlabeled files under /tmp and other directories. A local attacker could exploit a race window between the file discovery and the label change operation by swapping directory components with symlinks, causing chcon to follow the symlink and modify SELinux labels on arbitrary system files. This could undermine SELinux mandatory access control protections on critical files such as /etc/shadow.

Missing Authentication for Critical Function in Apache Texera (incubating).



The Python virtual environment (PVE) management endpoints of a computing unit are not authenticated by the application itself. In the local JVM and single-node Docker Compose deployments, which place no authenticating gateway in front of the services, these endpoints are reachable without credentials. The Kubernetes deployment gates them at the gateway, so only the Kubernetes deployment provides the full security model described in SECURITY.md.



This issue affects Apache Texera (incubating): from 1.1.0 through 1.2.0.



Users are recommended to use the Kubernetes deployment, which enforces the full security model, and to upgrade to 1.3.0-incubating, which documents that the local JVM and single-node Docker Compose deployments do not provide the full security model and should only be used by trusted users.

A flaw was found in GIMP. An integer overflow vulnerability exists when processing ICO image files, specifically in the `ico_read_info` and `ico_read_icon` functions. This issue arises because a size calculation for image buffers can wrap around due to a 32-bit integer evaluation, allowing oversized image headers to bypass security checks. A remote attacker could exploit this by providing a specially crafted ICO file, leading to a buffer overflow and memory corruption, which may result in an application level denial of service.

A flaw was found in GIMP's PSP (Paint Shop Pro) file parser. A remote attacker could exploit an integer overflow vulnerability in the read_creator_block() function by providing a specially crafted PSP image file. This vulnerability occurs when a 32-bit length value from the file is used for memory allocation without proper validation, leading to a heap overflow and an out-of-bounds write. Successful exploitation could result in an application level denial of service.

A flaw was found in p11-kit. A remote attacker could exploit this vulnerability by calling the C_DeriveKey function on a remote token with specific IBM kyber or IBM btc derive mechanism parameters set to NULL. This could lead to the RPC-client attempting to return an uninitialized value, potentially resulting in a NULL dereference or undefined behavior. This issue may cause an application level denial of service or other unpredictable system states.

cves.d: An incomplete fix for CVE-2024-47778 allows an out-of-bounds read in gst_wavparse_adtl_chunk() function. The patch added a size validation check lsize + 8 > size, but it does not account for the GST_ROUND_UP_2(lsize) used in the actual offset calculation. When lsize is an odd number, the parser advances more bytes than validated, causing OOB read.

XML::Sig versions before 0.74 for Perl allow code execution via a document's Algorithm attribute that verify resolves to a function name and calls.

The text after the last `#` in the DigestMethod and SignatureMethod Algorithm attributes is looked up with Digest::SHA->can. That returns a code reference for any fully qualified function name, Perl builtins in the CORE namespace included. The digest function is called on the canonical form of the referenced element, so the document picks both the function and its argument.

An attacker who can submit a signed document can run a command as the verifying process.

An information disclosure vulnerability in Zstandard versions 1.5.1 through 1.5.7 allows specially crafted compressed data to expose the contents of an internal buffer through decompressed output. The buffer is 64 KiB in the default configuration and may contain uninitialized memory or literals from earlier decompressions performed using the same decompression context. An attacker who can submit compressed data and observe the resulting output can recover the buffer's contents.
Various memory-safety issues in dataplane of SUSE Neuvector before 5.5, 5.5.0 before 5.5.6, 5.6.0 before 5.6.5 could be used by remote attackers to trigger crashes.

A flaw was found in libssh versions built with OpenSSL versions older than 3.0, specifically in the ssh_kdf() function responsible for key derivation. Due to inconsistent interpretation of return values where OpenSSL uses 0 to indicate failure and libssh uses 0 for success—the function may mistakenly return a success status even when key derivation fails. This results in uninitialized cryptographic key buffers being used in subsequent communication, potentially compromising SSH sessions' confidentiality, integrity, and availability.

A flaw was found in Podman. In a Containerfile or Podman, data written to RUN --mount=type=bind mounts during the podman build is not discarded. This issue can lead to files created within the container appearing in the temporary build context directory on the host, leaving the created files accessible.

There's a vulnerability in the libssh package where when a libssh consumer passes in an unexpectedly large input buffer to ssh_get_fingerprint_hash() function. In such cases the bin_to_base64() function can experience an integer overflow leading to a memory under allocation, when that happens it's possible that the program perform out of bounds write leading to a heap corruption.
This issue affects only 32-bits builds of libssh.

A vulnerability was found in systemd-coredump. This flaw allows an attacker to force a SUID process to crash and replace it with a non-SUID binary to access the original's privileged process coredump, allowing the attacker to read sensitive data, such as /etc/shadow content, loaded by the original process.

A SUID binary or process has a special type of permission, which allows the process to run with the file owner's permissions, regardless of the user executing the binary. This allows the process to access more restricted data than unprivileged users or processes would be able to. An attacker can leverage this flaw by forcing a SUID process to crash and force the Linux kernel to recycle the process PID before systemd-coredump can analyze the /proc/pid/auxv file. If the attacker wins the race condition, they gain access to the original's SUID process coredump file. They can read sensitive content loaded into memory by the original binary, affecting data confidentiality.
In crossbeam-channel rust crate, the internal `Channel` type's `Drop` method has a race condition which could, in some circumstances, lead to a double-free that could result in memory corruption.

A flaw was found in the FreeRDP used by Anaconda's remote install feature, where a crafted RDP packet could trigger a segmentation fault. This issue causes the service to crash and remain defunct, resulting in a denial of service. It occurs pre-boot and is likely due to a NULL pointer dereference. Rebooting is required to recover the system.

A flaw was found in Rust's Ring package. A panic may be triggered when overflow checking is enabled. In the QUIC protocol, this flaw allows an attacker to induce this panic by sending a specially crafted packet. It will likely occur unintentionally in 1 out of every 2**32 packets sent or received.

A flaw was found in systems utilizing LUKS-encrypted disks with GRUB configured for TPM-based auto-decryption. When GRUB is set to automatically decrypt disks using keys stored in the TPM, it reads the decryption key into system memory. If an attacker with physical access can corrupt the underlying filesystem superblock, GRUB will fail to locate a valid filesystem and enter rescue mode. At this point, the disk is already decrypted, and the decryption key remains loaded in system memory. This scenario may allow an attacker with physical access to access the unencrypted data without any further authentication, thereby compromising data confidentiality. Furthermore, the ability to force this state through filesystem corruption also presents a data integrity concern.

A flaw was found in GLib, which is vulnerable to an integer overflow in the g_string_insert_unichar() function. When the position at which to insert the character is large, the position will overflow, leading to a buffer underwrite.

A flaw was found in libsoup's SoupServer. A remote attacker could exploit a use-after-free vulnerability where the `soup_server_disconnect()` function frees connection objects prematurely, even if a TLS handshake is still pending. If the handshake completes after the connection object has been freed, a dangling pointer is accessed, leading to a server crash and a Denial of Service.

A flaw was found in libsoup. An integer underflow vulnerability occurs when processing content with a zero-length resource, leading to a buffer overread. This can allow an attacker to potentially access sensitive information or cause an application level denial of service.

A flaw was found in the ansible-core user module. When generate_ssh_key is enabled, User.ssh_key_gen() guards the key files against symlinks but checks the ~/.ssh directory only with os.path.exists(). An unprivileged user on a managed node who replaces their ~/.ssh with a symlink to an existing root-writable directory causes the privileged module to write the generated key pair through the symlink and then chown both files to that user. Because such files can be dropped into directories processed by schedulers (e.g. /etc/cron.daily) or dynamic MOTD (/etc/update-motd.d), the user can escalate to root on the managed node. This is an incomplete fix of CVE-2024-9902.

cves.d: A flaw was found in OpenSCAP. A heap-based buffer overflow can occur when processing a specially crafted Extensible Configuration Checklist Description Format (XCCDF) document using the sds-compose option. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability to corrupt memory, resulting in an application crash and a Denial of Service (DoS).

A flaw was found in Podman. An attacker can trigger a Denial of Service (DoS) by supplying a container image containing crafted metadata labels. Podman's auto-update mechanism improperly trusts these image labels to determine which system services to restart. If a user runs the malicious container and auto-update processes it, arbitrary system services are restarted with the user's privileges, potentially allowing an attacker to shut down the host system when Podman runs with administrative privileges.

A flaw was found in GStreamer's gst-plugins-bad package. A use of uninitialized memory vulnerability exists in the H.265 (HEVC) bitstream parser when processing Video Parameter Sets that declare more than one HRD (Hypothetical Reference Decoder) parameter set. A remote attacker could exploit this by providing a crafted H.265 media file or stream that, when processed by an application using GStreamer, causes unpredictable parser behavior and may crash the application. This can lead to a denial of service for any application using GStreamer to play back H.265 content.

A flaw was found in GStreamer's MXF demuxer plugin (gst-plugins-bad). When processing a specially crafted MXF media file, the demuxer indexes its internal delta-entry and slice-offset tables using values from the file without validating that they are within the bounds of the allocated arrays. A local attacker who tricks a user into opening a malicious MXF file can cause the application to crash (denial of service) and may be able to read limited amounts of heap memory adjacent to the affected arrays.

A flaw was found in the GStreamer JPEG 2000 decimator in gst-plugins-bad. Crafted JPEG 2000 media can cause integer overflows or division by zero during tile processing. An application that processes the malicious media may crash, resulting in a denial of service.

A flaw was found in libslirp in if_output(). When moving a session from the fast queue to the batch queue, the code unlinked and reinserted an arbitrary packet via ifm->m_nextpkt instead of the session queue head, corrupting queue pointers. A guest generating burst traffic could crash the host networking process, causing a denial of service.

A flaw was found in D-Bus. With a privileged Monitoring client attached (for example dbus-monitor or busctl monitor), an unprivileged local user can cause dbus-daemon to abort if a driver-originated broadcast such as NameOwnerChanged or ActivatableServicesChanged cannot be delivered to a recipient (for example due to a deny rule or an exceeded outgoing message queue). Driver broadcasts still use serial 0; when delivery fails, composing the monitor error reply asserts reply_serial != 0 and aborts the daemon.

A flaw was found in GStreamer's gst-plugins-base MicroDVD subtitle parser. When processing a specially crafted subtitle file, the parser may dereference a NULL pointer, causing the application to crash when a user opens or plays media with a malformed MicroDVD (.sub) subtitle file.

A flaw was found in GStreamer. An integer overflow vulnerability in the AV1 LEB128 variable-length integer parser allows a remote attacker to cause a crash in applications that process AV1 media content. By crafting a malformed AV1 bitstream containing an invalid LEB128-encoded value, an attacker can cause integer overflow in the parser, resulting in incorrect length values being used during stream processing, which can lead to a denial of service.

A flaw was found in the H.264 video parser in gst-plugins-bad. When processing a specially crafted H.264 video file or network stream with malformed Multiview (MVC) Sequence Parameter Set data, the parser can dereference a NULL pointer during the cleanup of partially allocated internal structures after a parse failure. This can cause the application using GStreamer to crash, resulting in a denial of service.

A flaw was found in GStreamer's gst-plugins-bad H.265 video parser. When parsing a specially crafted H.265 bitstream containing a Screen Content Coding (SCC) extension with certain palette predictor initializer settings, an integer underflow in the upper-bound computation allows the parser to accept an out-of-range value for the number of palette predictor entries. This causes the parser to write beyond the end of a fixed-size array, resulting in memory corruption and an application crash. An attacker can deliver the malformed bitstream as a local file or over a network stream such as HTTP, HLS, DASH, RTSP, RTP, or WebRTC. Successful exploitation requires the application to open or play that content, and is limited to a denial-of-service impact.

An unauthenticated attacker could trigger an Out of Memory condition to crash the Java process for RHCS by repeatedly sending HTTP requests to the TLS endpoint. Depending on how the RHCS server is configured, a manual intervention to restart it may prove necessary.

Uploading PDF files with active content to the languages form. The POST endpoint ‘/people/{person_id}/languages’ checks the declared MIME type and allows an authenticated user to upload a PDF with embedded JavaScript. The portal serves the file via a GET request to ‘/attachments/{attachment_id}’ with the ‘Content-Disposition: inline’ header, so it can be opened in the browser’s PDF viewer during review. The handling of active content depends on the viewer used.
A stack buffer overflow in DLP/WAF in the enforcer dataplane of SUSE NeuVector before 5.5, 5.5 before 5.5.6, 5.6.0 before 5.6.5 could be used by remote attackers to crash or potentially execute code.

TypesenseVectorStore is vulnerable to a document ID injection in its delete operation that can cause unintended documents to be deleted.



 TypesenseVectorStore.doDelete(List<String>) builds a Typesense filter_by expression by raw string concatenation of caller-supplied document IDs into the form id: [id1,id2,...] . The Typesense id field uses bare (unquoted) values in this list form with no escaping mechanism. An ID containing characters with syntactic meaning in the Typesense filter grammar — such as a comma ( , ), a closing bracket ( ] ), or operator tokens ( || , && ) — can break out of the list literal and alter the structure of the filter expression.



 An attacker who controls a document ID passed to the delete operation can use this to delete documents other than the intended ones (comma injection), or to construct a filter that matches every document in the collection (operator breakout), resulting in unintended bulk deletion.



 Applications that pass externally supplied or user-controlled document IDs to VectorStore.delete(List<String>) backed by TypesenseVectorStore are affected.

A flaw was found in Libsoup. The server-side digest authentication implementation in the SoupAuthDomainDigest class does not properly track issued nonces or enforce the required incrementing nonce-count (nc) attribute. This vulnerability allows a remote attacker to capture a single valid authentication header and replay it repeatedly. Consequently, the attacker can bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to protected resources, impersonating the legitimate user.

Stored Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) in 'carta_presentacion[contenido]' field in the POST request to '/personas/{persona_id}/cvs/{cv_id}/carta_presentaciones' on the job portal. The server stores the data entered by an authenticated candidate and displays it in the recruitment interface without sanitizing it. When reviewing an application, the recruiter’s browser can execute the injected JavaScript code within the context of their session on the portal.

A heap-based buffer overflow was found in Corosync's Totem SRP membership commit token handling. The sanity check for memb_commit_token messages validates only minimum length and address-entry counts, not an upper bound against the fixed commit_token_storage buffer. A network-adjacent attacker who can deliver a crafted oversized commit token to a node in the GATHER membership state may overflow the heap-allocated totemsrp instance, leading to memory corruption and denial of service.

A flaw was found in GIMP. Opening a crafted XCF with a truncated uncompressed tile can expose uninitialized main-process stack memory through the imported layer's pixel data, which may include process addresses that weaken ASLR.

A flaw was found in cyrus-sasl. When processing authentication requests using the Salted Challenge Response Authentication Mechanism (SCRAM), a remote attacker can trigger a null pointer dereference by submitting unexpected channel-binding data. This causes the server process to crash before validating authentication proofs, leading to a Denial of Service (DoS).

A flaw was found in lldpd. The service fails to verify that Link Layer Discovery Protocol - Media Endpoint Discovery (LLDP-MED) location records received from network neighbors match their declared lengths. An adjacent attacker on the local network can exploit this flaw by sending crafted packets, causing client applications using the liblldpctl library to read past buffer boundaries when parsing location data. This issue can lead to an information disclosure of adjacent process memory.

A path traversal flaw was found in ansible-core. When installing a collection with ansible-galaxy collection install, the install destination directory is derived from the namespace and name fields declared inside the collection artifact's own metadata, which are not validated as well-formed collection identifiers or checked for path containment. A malicious collection artifact -- delivered as a local file, a remote URL, a source directory, a git repository, or as a dependency -- can use a crafted name value to redirect the install destination outside the configured collections path, causing ansible-galaxy to delete an existing directory writable by the invoking user and then write attacker-controlled files to that location.

cves.d: An out-of-bounds read vulnerability was found in libsoup's multipart processing subsystem. The flaw exists in the soup_multipart_input_stream_read_headers() function inside soup-multipart-input-stream.c, which does not adequately restrict or validate the size of incoming multipart boundary strings. When processing a crafted HTTP response containing a malformed or oversized boundary parameter, the internal stream reader reads past the allocated buffer bounds. A remote, unauthenticated attacker can exploit this behavior to cause a service denial (DoS) through application failure or potentially read fragments of unauthorized memory metadata.

A flaw was found in libsoup's WebSocket implementation when using the permessage-deflate extension. The extension's decompression loop (inflate()) processes data in chunks without enforcing an upper boundary limit on the output buffer size. While libsoup limits the incoming compressed frame size via max_incoming_payload_size, it fails to track or limit memory allocation during decompression. A separate check for decompressed size (max_total_message_size) exists but executes only after inflation is complete, and it is entirely disabled by default for client connections. A remote, unauthenticated attacker can exploit this by sending a small, highly compressed payload (a decompression bomb), causing unbounded memory allocation that triggers an Out-of-Memory (OOM) crash and a Denial of Service (DoS).

A flaw was found in libarchive. This vulnerability allows a remote attacker to trigger a heap overflow by providing a specially crafted tar archive. The issue occurs during the parsing of a PAX extended header containing a malformed SUN.holesdata sparse-file attribute. Successful exploitation could lead to a denial of service, making the system unavailable, or potentially allow for arbitrary code execution, giving the attacker control over the affected system.

A flaw was found in the GNU Binutils (Binary Utilities) linker. This vulnerability, a heap-buffer-overflow read (CWE-125), occurs when the linker processes a specially crafted 32-bit XCOFF (Extended Common Object File Format) object file. An attacker could exploit this by providing a malicious file, leading to an out-of-bounds read of memory. This can result in information disclosure, potentially revealing sensitive heap data, and a Denial of Service (DoS) due to the linker crashing.

A flaw was found in 389-ds-base where the LDBM backend attribute encryption uses a hardcoded static initialization vector for AES-CBC and 3DES-CBC operations, allowing an attacker with privileged filesystem access to detect plaintext equality across encrypted entries by comparing ciphertext blocks.

normalizing a Distinguished Name (DN) that contains a legacy-quoted value encoding a
multivalued nested Relative Distinguished Name (RDN), the server can write past the
end of a heap allocation while sorting RDN attribute-value pairs. An unauthenticated
remote attacker can trigger this condition by sending an LDAP operation whose DN
reaches the DN normalization routine, such as a search with a crafted base DN. This
can corrupt heap memory and may cause denial of service.

cves.d: A flaw was found in the libsoup HTTP library that can cause proxy authentication credentials to be sent to unintended destinations. When handling HTTP redirects, libsoup removes the Authorization header but does not remove the Proxy-Authorization header if the request is redirected to a different host. As a result, sensitive proxy credentials may be leaked to third-party servers. Applications using libsoup for HTTP communication may unintentionally expose proxy authentication data.

A flaw was found in libsoup. An attacker who can control the input for the Content-Disposition header can inject CRLF (Carriage Return Line Feed) sequences into the header value. These sequences are then interpreted verbatim when the HTTP request or response is constructed, allowing arbitrary HTTP headers to be injected. This vulnerability can lead to HTTP header injection or HTTP response splitting without requiring authentication or user interaction.

A flaw was found in GLib. An integer overflow vulnerability in its Unicode case conversion implementation can lead to memory corruption. By processing specially crafted and extremely large Unicode strings, an attacker could trigger an undersized memory allocation, resulting in out-of-bounds writes. This could cause applications utilizing GLib for string conversion to crash or become unstable.

A flaw was found in the GLib Base64 encoding routine when processing very large input data. Due to incorrect use of integer types during length calculation, the library may miscalculate buffer boundaries. This can cause memory writes outside the allocated buffer. Applications that process untrusted or extremely large Base64 input using GLib may crash or behave unpredictably.

A flaw was found in libsoup, an HTTP client library. This vulnerability, known as CRLF (Carriage Return Line Feed) Injection, occurs when an HTTP proxy is configured and the library improperly handles URL-decoded input used to create the Host header. A remote attacker can exploit this by providing a specially crafted URL containing CRLF sequences, allowing them to inject additional HTTP headers or complete HTTP request bodies. This can lead to unintended or unauthorized HTTP requests being forwarded by the proxy, potentially impacting downstream services.

A flaw was found in open-iscsi. An integer underflow vulnerability in the `iscsiuio` component, specifically during IPv4 Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) parsing, allows a remote attacker on the same local network segment to cause a denial of service. By sending a specially crafted IPv4/UDP DHCP reply, the attacker can trigger an out-of-bounds read, leading to the `iscsiuio` process crashing. This issue affects systems where `iscsiuio` is actively handling IPv4 DHCP traffic.

A flaw was found in open-iscsi's iscsiuio component. This vulnerability involves an integer underflow and out-of-bounds read during Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6 (DHCPv6) packet parsing. Specifically, crafted DHCPv6 Advertise traffic with a short User Datagram Protocol (UDP) length can cause the DHCPv6 payload length to underflow. An unauthenticated attacker on an adjacent network segment can exploit this by sending specially crafted IPv6 UDP traffic while the client is in an active DHCPv6 exchange, leading to a denial of service due to a process crash or service disruption.

A flaw was found in open-iscsi. This vulnerability allows a remote attacker on the same local network segment to cause a Denial of Service (DoS) in the iscsiuio daemon. By sending a specially crafted Internet Control Message Protocol version 6 (ICMPv6) Router Advertisement with a zero-length option, the attacker can trigger an infinite loop. This leads to sustained CPU usage, rendering the daemon unresponsive and impacting system availability. A secondary risk of out-of-bounds reads exists with a short IPv6 payload, though no memory corruption or data exposure has been confirmed.

A flaw was found in 389-ds-base. The get_ldapmessage_controls_ext() function frees the parsed controls array on the Session Tracking critical-control rejection path without clearing the SLAPI_REQCONTROLS pblock slot. Operation teardown then frees the same pointer again, causing a double-free. An unauthenticated remote attacker can trigger this with a single BIND request carrying a critical Session Tracking control, resulting in heap corruption and potential denial of service.

A flaw was found in 389 Directory Server. During SASL PLAIN authentication, the server installs connection-level bind credentials before performing the account-lock check. If the account is subsequently found to be locked, the bind is reported as failed to the client, but the already-installed authenticated state on the connection is not reverted. A client that supplies valid credentials for an account that has been administratively locked can continue to use the same connection with that account's privileges, defeating account lock as an access-revocation control.

A flaw was found in libtiff. A heap-buffer overflow vulnerability exists in the `tiff2pdf` utility due to an integer truncation error when processing crafted BigTIFF files. An attacker can provide a specially crafted BigTIFF file, causing a 64-bit `StripByteCounts` value to be truncated to a 32-bit integer. This leads to an undersized memory allocation and a subsequent out-of-bounds memory copy, resulting in a crash and severe memory corruption.

A flaw was found in Dogtag PKI's ACME responder where the HTTP-01 challenge validator accepts IP address literals as dns identifiers and follows HTTP redirects without validating that the target is a public address. An unauthenticated ACME account holder can exploit this to perform server-side request forgery (SSRF), making the Dogtag server send HTTP GET requests to internal network services. With the InMemory database backend, the response body of internal targets is disclosed to the attacker through the ACME challenge error.

When the daemon is running in system mode with RDP enabled, the incoming connection handler bypasses the connection throttler, allowing an unauthenticated remote attacker to open many parallel pre-authentication connections to the RDP listener. cves.d:
A flaw was found in CRIU's handling of restartable sequences (rseq) during checkpoint/restore. A malicious process inside a container can register an rseq critical section that hijacks CRIU's parasite code injection during checkpoint, allowing it to spoof the process credentials saved in the checkpoint image. On restore, the container process gains elevated capabilities and zeroed UIDs/GIDs.

The practical impact on Red Hat products is limited by several factors: checkpoint/restore requires root privileges (podman) or cluster-admin RBAC (OpenShift) to trigger and cannot be initiated from within the container itself; on OpenShift prior to 4.17 the feature required explicit opt-in, and on 4.17+ the kubelet checkpoint API RBAC is not configured by default; OpenShift enforces user namespaces by default for regular workloads (hostUsers is gated behind admin-only SCCs), which makes the spoofed capabilities namespace-scoped and ineffective for privilege escalation; SELinux type enforcement (container_t) blocks privilege transitions independently of capabilities; seccomp filters persist through checkpoint/restore and cannot be corrupted via the parasite; and kernel mount namespace ownership checks on RHEL 9/10 kernels prevent mount-based container escape even with spoofed capabilities.

A flaw was found in Dogtag PKI's ACME responder where the web.xml security constraints use exact URL pattern matching for admin-only enable/disable endpoints. By appending a trailing slash to the URL, an unauthenticated attacker can bypass the Tomcat authentication constraint while RESTEasy still routes the request to the handler, allowing unauthorized toggling of the ACME service state including persistent denial of service.

A flaw was found in gdk-pixbuf. When parsing a specially crafted ICO file with pixel values that exceed the defined palette range, an out-of-bounds read can occur due to improper bounds checking against the actual palette size. This vulnerability causes heap bytes to be interpreted as valid palette indices and rendered as RGB pixel values in the output image, allowing an attacker to extract heap content via the generated output, such as a thumbnail.

A path traversal vulnerability in the File Explorer share-link folder-listing endpoint allows a remote attacker with a folder-scoped share link to list directory contents outside the shared folder, including other Samba shares readable by the link creator, because path validation occurs before path canonicalization.
Affected products and versions include: from ADM 4.1.0 through ADM 4.3.3.RY62 as well as from ADM 5.0.0 through ADM 5.1.4.RM62.

A heap-buffer-overflow flaw was found in Directory Server (389-ds-base). When a DN contains a legacy-quoted value, the server won't close the heap allocation allowing another call to refer to the same memory pointer causing a denial of service or an arbitrary memory write operation.

An unauthenticated remote attacker can exploit a path traversal vulnerability in the PCP pmproxy logger servlet using a crafted hostname. This allows arbitrary file and directory creation, potentially leading to a denial of service.

A flaw was found in the PCP (Performance Co-Pilot) `pmproxy` service. A remote attacker can exploit a vulnerability in the `pmLogLoadInDom()` function by sending a specially crafted request. This bypasses a critical bounds check, which can lead to the `pmproxy` service crashing, causing a Denial of Service (DoS). Additionally, this flaw may enable the leakage of sensitive information from the system's memory.

A flaw was found in the sbc library (BlueZ SBC codec). An off-by-one error in the SBC frame decoder allows a crafted audio payload to trigger a one-byte heap out-of-bounds read. This could allow an adjacent attacker streaming Bluetooth audio to read a single byte of adjacent heap memory.

A stack-based buffer overflow was found in rpcbind's rpcinfo utility. In rpcbdump() short mode (used by `rpcinfo -s`), version numbers from a remote RPCBPROC_DUMP reply are written into a fixed-size stack buffer without bounds checking. A user or administrator who runs `rpcinfo -s` against a malicious or compromised rpcbind endpoint could experience a crash or denial of service of the rpcinfo client.

An OS command injection vulnerability in ADM allows an authenticated administrator to create an iSCSI LUN with a crafted name and schedule a snapshot. The scheduler embeds the name in a root cron job without correctly neutralizing shell metacharacters, allowing arbitrary command execution as root when the job runs.
Affected products and versions include: from ADM 4.1.0 through ADM 4.3.3.RY62 as well as from ADM 5.0.0 through ADM 5.1.4.RM62.

An improper input validation vulnerability in the OpenVPN client configuration import feature of ADM allows authenticated administrative users to execute arbitrary operating system commands via a crafted .ovpn profile.
Affected products and versions include: from ADM 4.1.0 through ADM 4.3.3.RY62 as well as from ADM 5.0.0 through ADM 5.1.4.RM62.

A stack-based buffer overflow was found in rpcbind's rpcinfo utility. When querying a remote rpcbind service with `rpcinfo -l`, address information returned by the server is copied into a fixed-size buffer without sufficient bounds checking. A malicious or compromised rpcbind server could use this flaw to crash the rpcinfo client, resulting in a denial of service. The highest threat from this vulnerability is to system availability.

A path traversal vulnerability in the File Explorer share-link upload component allows a remote attacker with a folder-scoped upload share link to upload or overwrite files in the shared folder's immediate parent directory due to missing trailing validation prior to path canonicalization.
Affected products and versions include: from ADM 4.1.0 through ADM 4.3.3.RY62 as well as from ADM 5.0.0 through ADM 5.1.4.RM62.

A flaw was found in xdgmime. A heap-based buffer overflow can be triggered in _xdg_mime_magic_parse_magic_line() in the xdgmimemagic.c file on little-endian systems when an attacker-controlled MIME magic file in a user-writable XDG data location (e.g., in the $XDG_DATA_HOME/mime/magic path) is parsed by an application performing MIME type detection (e.g., via g_content_type_guess()). When performing byte-swap, incorrect pointer arithmetic on the write side causes an out-of-bounds write of 2 bytes, resulting in an application crash or memory corruption.
